title: Who checks the records?
text: In 1951, a British businessman called Sir Hugh Beaver was out hunting in Ireland when he got into an argument with his friends. They wanted to know which was the fastest game bird in Europe, but none of the reference books in the house could give them an answer. Beaver, who was the managing director of the Guinness brewery, realised that people in pubs all over the country must be having similar arguments every night. What they needed, he thought, was a book that could settle them.

To write it, he hired two twin brothers, Norris and Ross McWhirter, who ran a fact-finding agency in London and were known for their extraordinary memory for facts and figures. The first edition of the Guinness Book of Records was published in 1955. To the surprise of almost everyone, it became a bestseller by Christmas. Since then, the book has been translated into dozens of languages, and it is now one of the best-selling books in the world.

But a book of records is only useful if people can trust it. Today, that responsibility belongs to a team of official adjudicators, the judges who decide whether a record has really been broken. Their job takes them all over the world, from schools and shopping centres to television studios, and they may spend one day counting hula hoops and the next measuring the longest fingernails on the planet.

Breaking a record is not as simple as doing something impressive. First, the challenger must apply and receive a set of guidelines, which explain exactly how the attempt must be carried out. These rules can be surprisingly strict. For a food record, for example, all of the food usually has to be eaten afterwards rather than wasted. For a distance record, the measuring equipment may need to be checked by an expert beforehand.

Not every attempt has an adjudicator present. Many people instead send in evidence, such as videos, photographs and statements from independent witnesses, which is then carefully examined by the team. This process can take several weeks, and many applications are rejected, often because a small rule was not followed. Some challengers are disappointed, but the adjudicators insist that the rules are what give a record its value.

Certain records are no longer accepted at all. Over the years, the organisation has stopped monitoring challenges that could put people or animals in danger, such as eating the most of something in a very short time or making a pet as heavy as possible. The aim, they say, is to celebrate achievement, not to encourage people to harm themselves.

Interestingly, the question that started it all has never been fully answered. The fastest game bird in Europe is often said to be the golden plover, but experts still disagree about how such a thing should be measured. Perhaps that is fitting. As the adjudicators know better than anyone, a record is only as good as the evidence behind it.
